title: Light-source detectives
subtitle: Spring 2 • Week 1 • Sort the evidence, not the shine
objective: Distinguish objects that give out their own light from surfaces that reflect light.

sow.exactOutcome: Identify sources of light and surfaces that reflect light.
sow.alignment: Direct match to the named outcome. The lesson is a 40-minute exemplar, with optional greater depth; no accreditation completion is claimed.

priorLearning: Everyday objects can be described by what we observe.
Use a labelled diagram or evidence card to explain a choice.
success: Use evidence to classify a source or reflector.
Explain how a non-glowing object can be seen.
Recognise reflection from both mirrors and ordinary surfaces.

vocabulary.meaning: Something that gives out its own light.

equipment: Printed object cards; low-power LED torch; white paper; unbreakable mirror; dark fabric; optional switched-on screen.
preparation: Print the six evidence cards. Check an unbreakable mirror for sharp edges.
If demonstrating reflection, keep the beam on a desk or screen, away from faces.
safety: Use a low-power cool LED only. No lasers, hot lamps or direct Sun viewing.
Use an unbreakable mirror and keep reflected light away from eyes. Do not darken the room fully.
practicalAlternative: Sort the six supplied cases and trace the supplied mirror and paper diagrams; no practical is needed.

misconceptions.correction: A shiny surface can reflect light from another source.
misconceptions.check: Ask what happens when no light reaches the mirror.

misconceptions.correction: Ordinary paper and other visible non-glowing objects reflect light too.
misconceptions.check: Ask how light from paper reaches the eye.

misconceptions.claim: The Moon is a light source in this classification.
misconceptions.correction: The Moon is seen mainly by reflected sunlight; it does not make that visible light.

access.supported: Choose one route: short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed explanation; keep the same science goal.
access.standard: Use the evidence provided to record a decision and explain the science in short sentences.
access.stretch: Apply the same core idea to a changed setup, identify a limitation and justify a better decision.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence and equipment. Offer seated observation, a quiet paper route, partner rehearsal and a pass. Never require public performance or a darkened room.

sources.title: Department for Education: science programmes of study
sources.note: Checked 8 September 2026. Year 3 light outcomes anchor the BUILD content; ray explanations are carefully modelled as an accessible extension.

slides.title: Does bright mean source?
body: Did their light start in the same place?
slides.notes: Invite a prediction without settling it. State that source means gives out its own visible light here. Objects can also reflect while emitting; we classify the stated situation.

slides.title: Follow the light
body: 1. What do we need to see?
3. Does an unlit plain card glow?
slides.notes: Answers: light; yes; no. If needed trace one source→object→eye path from the previous lesson.

slides.title: I ask where the light began
body: The lit lamp gives out light.
It reflects some of that light.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I do not sort by bright or shiny. I ask whether this object gives out its own light. The lamp does. The plain card returns some arriving light.” A source can also reflect; the card’s reflected light began elsewhere.

visual.title: Make light or reflect it?
visual.description: A lit lamp gives out its own visible light. A non-luminous card reflects some light arriving from that lamp. Both can be seen when light reaches an eye.

elements.text:
Source: gives out
its own light.

Reflector: returns some
light that reaches it.

slides.title: A mirror redirects light
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I trace the arrows towards the mirror, then away. The mirror changes the direction; it does not switch on its own supply of light.” Diagram uses equal incident/reflection angles qualitatively; no angle calculation required.

visual.title: A mirror changes the light direction
visual.description: A ray travels down and right onto a horizontal mirror, then up and right towards a screen; incident and reflected angles are equal in this schematic.

elements.text: The mirror reflects light; it does not make the light.

slides.title: Paper reflects too
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “I can see the ordinary paper because light reaches my eyes from it. The arrows leave in several directions. Reflection does not always give a clear image.” Arrow counts are not measured amounts.

visual.title: Ordinary paper reflects light too
visual.description: A source ray reaches a rough paper surface; reflected rays leave in several directions. This is a schematic of diffuse reflection, not a ray traced from one perfectly flat point.

elements.text: A clear mirror image is not needed for reflection.

slides.title: Sort the evidence cards
body: Give a clue, then swap roles.
slides.notes: Place two headings on the desk. Partners take reader and sorter roles, swapping after three cards. Use the evidence rather than memory alone. A/C/E source; B/D/F reflector.

rows: Lit LED lamp; gives out light
White paper; lit by room light
table.caption: Constructed teaching evidence

slides.reveal: A, C and E give out their own light in these cases.

slides.title: The switch-off challenge
body: The phone screen is now off.
slides.notes: Hold up or describe an unlit phone screen. Let each pair revise one classification. In this stated off case the screen reflects room light, so it can still be visible. Also ask about the mirror in no light: it cannot create a view.
slides.prompt: W2. How does switching off change our account?
slides.reveal: The off screen can reflect room light. It no longer supplies its own display light.

slides.title: Which statement works?
body: Choose one and give a reason.
slides.notes: If only mirrors are credited with reflection, return to the paper diagram. If Moon is selected as source, ask pupils to trace the light backwards to the Sun without looking at it.

options.text: All shiny objects make their own light.
options.feedback: Shiny surfaces such as mirrors reflect arriving light.

options.text: Only a mirror can reflect light.
options.feedback: Paper and many other surfaces reflect light too.

options.text: We can see paper when reflected light reaches our eyes.
options.feedback: Paper reflects some light from a source into the eye.

slides.title: Choose your investigation route
slides.notes: Give one route only, selected with the pupil. The shared evidence page supports every route. Optional paper-and-mirror observation is supporting evidence; card sorting provides the full independent route. Avoid treating the classes as mutually exclusive for every possible object or condition.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Read or point to one clue.
slides.notes: Shares the 12-minute independent stage. Optional paper-and-mirror observation is supporting evidence; card sorting provides the full independent route. Avoid treating the classes as mutually exclusive for every possible object or condition.

slides.title: Make your own science record
body: Use a diagram, words or speech.
Check one answer with the evidence.
slides.notes: Allow ten minutes of independent response after the two-minute setup. Optional paper-and-mirror observation is supporting evidence; card sorting provides the full independent route. Avoid treating the classes as mutually exclusive for every possible object or condition.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: Does my answer match the evidence?
slides.notes: Shares the independent stage. Ask the pupil to point to the clue supporting their answer; accept a spoken correction or changed choice.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve our account
body: Choose how to share one idea.
Use evidence to improve our account.
slides.notes: Give a private or paired option. Adopt one scientifically sound pupil revision in the class explanation and name the change. No public ranking.
slides.prompt: How should we replace “bright means source”?
slides.reveal: Ask: does it give out its own light, or reflect light arriving from elsewhere?

slides.title: Three quick checks
body: E1. What is a light source?
E2. Does ordinary paper reflect light?
E3. Does the Moon make the sunlight we see from it?
slides.notes: Collect brief individual answers. Secure core requires the main idea and a relevant reason. Revisit the relevant worked diagram next lesson if the explanation reverses cause and effect.
slides.reveal: See the teacher answer guide for the three checks.

pupilPages.title: Evidence: six light cases
pupilPages.intro: Constructed teaching cards. Classify the stated case.

cards.title: A • Lit LED lamp
cards.text: The switched-on LED gives out visible light.

cards.title: B • Moon
cards.text: Sunlight reaches the Moon. Some is reflected towards Earth.

cards.title: C • Phone screen on
cards.text: The working display gives out visible light.

cards.title: D • Mirror
cards.text: Room light reaches the mirror and is reflected.

cards.title: E • Firefly
cards.text: This insect produces light through a chemical reaction in its body.

cards.title: F • White paper
cards.text: A lamp lights the ordinary paper. The paper reflects some light.

blocks.prompt: W1. Which cards describe sources? Give one clue.
W2. The phone screen is off in a lit room. How can it still be seen?

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Sort and explain
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: source / reflects / light / eye.

blocks.prompt: S2. Card D __ light from the room.
S3. Put B and F in the source or reflector group.
S4. Explain how light from paper reaches the eye.
S5. Name one source that is a living thing, using the cards.

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Make a display label
pupilPages.intro: Use the card evidence, not brightness or shine.

blocks.prompt: T2. Write a label explaining how a mirror can look bright.
T3. Draw a source → paper → eye light path.

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Challenge the rule
pupilPages.intro: A display says: “If it shines, it must be a source.”

blocks.prompt: X1. Use a card to show why this rule fails.
X2. Replace it with a better sorting question.
X3. Compare the phone screen on and off in a lit room.
X4. A mirror is placed in a box with no light at all. Predict whether it can light the box. Explain.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. What is a light source?
E2. Does ordinary paper reflect light?
E3. Does the Moon make the sunlight we see from it?
R1. Which idea did you improve after hearing evidence?
R2. What would you investigate or ask next?

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: Light; light enters the eye; ordinary unlit card does not glow.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 A, C and E sources; B, D and F reflectors. W2 an off screen can reflect room light although it no longer emits display light.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: Third option correct. Mirrors do not create the reflected light; reflection also occurs at non-shiny surfaces.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 source. S2 reflects. S3 B and F reflectors. S4 source light reaches paper and some reflected light enters the eye. S5 firefly.

answers.label: T1–T3
answers.answer: T1 A source; B reflector; C source; D reflector; E source; F reflector. T2 mirror returns some arriving light towards the eye. T3 arrows from source to paper and from paper towards eye.

answers.label: X1–X4
answers.answer: X1 the bright mirror reflects light. X2 ask whether the object gives out its own light in this stated condition. X3 on screen emits display light and can also reflect; off screen can still reflect room light. X4 no: with no incoming light it cannot illuminate the box.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 gives out its own light. E2 yes. E3 no, it reflects sunlight.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a science-related revision or relevant next question. A pass or private response is acceptable; preferences have no fixed right answer.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 7; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 12; review 3; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the stage time.
BUILD follows the user’s Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful materials for secondary pupils. Routes are adjustable access choices, not fixed groups or diagnoses.
Every core task can run from the printed evidence. Do not present constructed teaching evidence as observations pupils made. A pupil’s spoken reasoning carries the same scientific value as writing.
The word source can be used differently in advanced optics. Here it means a primary visible-light emitter, matching the elementary curriculum distinction. Accept that lit sources can reflect too.

HTML We do: pupils choose a prediction, test it against the user-controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. The shared paper cases and W1/W2 prompts provide the equivalent classroom discussion without a device. Any animation is a teaching model, not filmed experimental evidence.

interactive.title: Source or reflector: evidence challenge
interactive.intro: Make a choice, test it against the stated evidence, then trace where the light began.

steps.question: Card A is a switched-on LED lamp. How is it supplying light?

choices.text: It gives out its own light
choices.feedback: The lit LED is a source in this case.
The card explicitly says the switched-on LED emits visible light.

visual.title: Make light or reflect it?
visual.description: A lit lamp gives out its own visible light. A non-luminous card reflects some light arriving from that lamp. Both can be seen when light reaches an eye.

elements.text:
Source: gives out
its own light.

Reflector: returns some
light that reaches it.

steps.explanation: Card A is a source. Card F, ordinary paper, reflects some light that reaches it.

steps.question: Card D is a mirror lit by room light. Where did its reflected light begin?

choices.feedback: The mirror is reflecting light, not generating the light in this case.

visual.title: A mirror changes the light direction
visual.description: A ray travels down and right onto a horizontal mirror, then up and right towards a screen; incident and reflected angles are equal in this schematic.

elements.text: The mirror reflects light; it does not make the light.

steps.explanation: A mirror changes direction. It needs arriving light to provide this reflected path.

steps.question: Card F is plain white paper. Can it reflect light without a clear mirror image?

choices.feedback: Rough surfaces can reflect in many directions.
Reflection also happens at ordinary non-shiny surfaces.

visual.title: Ordinary paper reflects light too
visual.description: A source ray reaches a rough paper surface; reflected rays leave in several directions. This is a schematic of diffuse reflection, not a ray traced from one perfectly flat point.

elements.text: A clear mirror image is not needed for reflection.

steps.explanation: Reflection need not form a clear image. Paper can be seen when some reflected light enters the eye.
